opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the most useful thing is to treat it like onboarding notes for a new teammate who's very capable but has never seen your codebase before. The agent can read code well, so you don't need to explain everything. What it can't easily infer is the tribal knowledge.

The first thing I'd put in is how to verify work: how to run the tests, which test commands are fast and which are slow, how to run the linter or type checker, and what "done" looks like for a change. If Codex knows how to check its own work, the quality of what comes back goes up dramatically, because it can iterate until things actually pass instead of handing you something that looks plausible.

Second, the layout of the repo and where things live. Something like "the API handlers are here, shared utilities are there, don't touch this generated directory." That saves a lot of wasted exploration, especially in a big monorepo.

Third, conventions and preferences that aren't obvious from the code. Maybe you prefer a certain error-handling pattern, or there's a library you're migrating away from and you don't want new code using it. Those are things a human engineer would learn in code review over a few weeks, and you can just write them down once.

I'd also say keep it concise and keep it current. People sometimes dump huge amounts of documentation in there, and it becomes noise. It works best when it's short, specific, and actionable. A nice habit is that whenever you find yourself correcting the agent about the same thing twice, that's a signal it belongs in agents.md.

You can also nest them, with a top-level file for the whole repo and more specific ones in subdirectories for particular components. That keeps the guidance close to where it matters.

r001.rationale: It recommends documenting where key parts of the repository live and says this saves wasted exploration, especially in a large monorepo.

r002.rationale: It explicitly recommends recording conventions and preferences that are not obvious from the code.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is: an agents.md is the stuff you'd tell a new engineer on their first day that they couldn't figure out from just reading the code. That's the filter.

So the most useful things, honestly, are the practical ones. How do I build this thing, how do I run the tests, and specifically how do I run one test or one package rather than the whole suite, because the model will want to iterate quickly and if it only knows the slow command it'll waste a lot of time. Any linters or formatters you expect to be run before something is considered done. That alone gets you a huge chunk of the value, because Codex will actually go verify its own work if it knows how.

The second category is the stuff that's really about your codebase's conventions and taste. Where do things live, what's the layering, "don't put business logic in this directory," "we use this pattern for errors, not that one." Those are things that aren't obvious from any single file and that the model would otherwise have to rediscover every time, or get subtly wrong.

And then the third thing, which people underuse, is telling it what not to touch and how you want it to behave. Like, "don't modify the generated files, regenerate them with this command." Or "when you're unsure, prefer a smaller diff." Or "always add a test when you fix a bug." You're basically encoding the review feedback you'd otherwise give over and over.

What I'd say to avoid is making it a giant document. It's not documentation, it's not a style guide dump. If it's too long the signal gets diluted, and honestly the model reads the code pretty well on its own now. So keep it short, keep it concrete, and treat it as a living thing: when Codex does something you don't like twice, that's a line that should go into agents.md. And you can nest them, so a monorepo can have a top-level one and then more specific ones per package, which keeps each one focused.

r001.rationale: It mentions guidance on where things live and what is not obvious from reading code, but does not describe this as a compressed alternative to exploring the entire codebase.

r002.rationale: It recommends documenting codebase conventions and preferences that are not obvious from the code itself.

astra-6.text:
I’d put in the things that help Codex get oriented in your codebase: how the repository is organized, how to run the relevant tests, and any conventions you expect it to follow. If there’s a particular way to build the project, or generated files it shouldn’t edit directly, make that explicit.

The most useful guidance is concrete and actionable. Think about what you’d tell an engineer on their first day so they can make a change and verify it. Keep it concise and up to date, so the important instructions are easy to find.

r001.rationale: The response recommends describing repository organization to help Codex get oriented, but does not say this guidance compresses or replaces exploring the entire codebase.

r002.rationale: It recommends documenting conventions Codex should follow, but does not specify that these preferences belong in agents.md when they are not apparent from the codebase.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d put in the things that are specific to your repository and hard for the agent to infer: how to run the tests, which commands to use to build the project, and the conventions you want it to follow. If there are architectural boundaries—this module shouldn’t depend on that one—or generated files it shouldn’t edit, those are useful to spell out too.

I’d keep it concise and actionable. Think about what you’d tell a new teammate before their first change. And as you use Codex, if you find yourself correcting the same thing repeatedly, that’s a good candidate to add.

r001.rationale: The response gives examples of repository guidance but does not describe it as a compressed substitute for exploring the entire codebase.

r002.rationale: It recommends recording repository-specific guidance that is hard to infer, including conventions the user wants Codex to follow.
